prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and thereby transforming the analysis of the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: B001 is the discovery I find most persuasive on conceptual novelty, attribution and maturity together. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) replaced the representative-firm view with selection of heterogeneous firms into exporting and FDI. That changed what is meant by gains from trade: reallocation across firms and productivity selection became first-order channels. It also redirected empirical work toward firm-level microdata, and the framework is now standard in teaching, quantification and trade-policy evaluation. More than twenty years of replication and extension mean the central mechanism has been tested rather than merely admired. Credit is concentrated in two people: Melitz for the core model, and Helpman for the monopolistic-competition foundations and the exports-versus-FDI sorting result. I hold this view on the merits of the discovery. I do not count how many colleagues ranked it first, and I do not think the Committee should.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Parallel and complementary contributors (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum) are outside the credited names, and Redding's quantitative and spatial work is credited on the ballot but excluded from my pair. A two-person prize therefore leaves out some who shaped the field. Some detailed predictions of the baseline Melitz model are rejected in firm-level data, and much of the model's influence comes from its extensions. Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work also sits close to the lineage recognised in 2008. The Committee could reasonably judge that part of this credit is already covered.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the BLP demand and dynamic-oligopoly estimation work (B006) first. He argues it is fully mature and that merger review, antitrust, trade and environmental policy depend on it. He ranks B001 second and notes the attribution difficulties around Redding and the empirical contributors.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and breadth of B006, and I rank it third. It is my first alternative, and we agree that the BLP core of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is well attributed. Two things keep it below B001 for me. First, the ballot bundles demand estimation, dynamic games and entry models across seven credited names, so the boundary of the discovery is looser than B001's. Second, much of B006's impact is that of an estimation toolkit, whereas B001 also changed the economic content of trade theory: who exports, who gains and who loses. I would not call this a decisive difference. If the Committee judges that tool-building of this kind should carry equal weight, B006 would be a legitimate preferred part.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B006 first and B001 second. He stresses that industrial organisation has not been recognised since 2014 and trade not since 2008. He also says Redding's quantitative work is more derivative and that the omitted Bernard-Eaton-Kortum-Jensen group is an attribution risk.
responses.response: I agree on Redding and on the attribution risk, and I have listed both as open uncertainties. I would not give weight to how recently a field was honoured when comparing merit across subfields. That argument does not discriminate between B001 and B006, since both fields have waited similarly long. It would also make the decision depend on rotation rather than on the discovery. So I rest my preference on the scientific case and treat the timing point as neutral.

responses.point: Krusell proposes only Persson and Tabellini for the political-economics entry (B038). He judges it to complement the 2024 institutions prize without overlapping it, and he treats Besley as a more separate strand on state capacity and political agency.
responses.response: I proposed three names for B038 in my opening and I see merit in his narrower pairing, since Persson and Tabellini are the closest to one research programme. I disagree that overlap with 2024 is clearly small. The 2024 prize concerned institutions and long-run prosperity, and B038 asks how constitutions and electoral rules shape fiscal outcomes. These are different questions but they overlap in the underlying literature. The cross-country identification of constitutional effects is also weaker than the evidence behind B001. This is why B038 is not among my preferred parts or alternatives, even though I ranked it fourth.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and proposes Helpman and Melitz, leaving out Redding because his work is a later extension. He also asks whether the Committee would rather add Redding or empirical pioneers who are not on the ballot.
responses.response: I agree with his two-name attribution and his reasoning on Redding. I would go further: quantitative and spatial trade models are better judged as a separate achievement than as a third name added to B001. Adding Redding here would blur a currently clean citation. Empirical pioneers outside the credited list cannot be added by this Committee under the ballot as constituted, and I would not use their absence as a reason to enlarge the prize. I would treat it only as a caveat on completeness of credit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee should credit Redding, or the parallel empirical and quantitative-trade contributors, alongside or instead of Helpman and Melitz.
How much of the Helpman credit overlaps with the monopolistic-competition lineage already recognised in 2008.
Whether B030 or B006 would be better as a second, distinct achievement if the Committee wants a two-part prize. Any such addition would have to fit within three unique people.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority records or award histories, and my assessments rest on the supplied evidence and general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows co-authorship with Torsten Persson and Bo Rothstein (a corruption paper in Governance), and Persson is a credited name on B038. I also gave the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity, which is thematically adjacent to B038. B038 is not in my preferred configuration or alternatives, so this has no bearing on my proposal. No connection to the credited names on B001, B030 or B006 is apparent from the supplied profile.
